SHRI B.P. SINGHAL: Sir,4n the statement which has been given by the 
hon. Minister, there is a wide difference in the time taken in the construction of 
various flyovers. There are as many as six instances where work worth Rs. 1 
crore has been done every month. Sir, Rs. one crore worth of job has been done 
per month. Whereas in some cases, for completing a job worth of even half a 
crore, the time taken is about two years. Sir, in cases where the estimated 
expenditure was even 40 per cent or 50 pe r cent higher, the job was done in a 
time which was less than the time taken for completing smaller work. So, I want 
to know whether any reward was given to the concerned agencies for reducing 
the amount rather than actually spending it. In two cases, i.e., in the construction 
of the IIT Flyover and the Chirag Delhi Flyover, the expenses went up by 40 per 
cent or even in some cases by 50 per cent. Was any penalty imposed on those 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [29 April, 2002] 
agencies for this cost overrun, which are responsible for it? These are the three 
points on which 1 would like the Minister to comment. 
SHRI ANANTH KUMAR: Sir, there are multiple agencies in Delhi which 
are executing the work of various flyovers. In Delhi, there are 32 flyovers which 
have already been constructed, and there are still 12 flyovers where the work is 
in progress. In addition to these, the work on 23 flyovers is under 
conceptualisation, which means, these flyovers are in pipeline. Sir, the agencies 
which are involved in the construction of various flyovers are : PWD, DDA, 
MCD, NDMC, and surprisingly, Sir, even the Delhi Tourism Development 
Corporation is also involved in this. So, Sir, you can see the multiplicity of 
agencies which are involv ed in carrying out the construction work of these 
flyovers in Delhi. I appreciate the con cern of the senior hon. Member of the 
House for raising the question as to why the time over-run and cost run are so 
high, and what measures are being taken by the Government. Sir, as the nodal 
Ministry and half-nodal Ministry to all these agencies, I would like to say that 
I will convene a meeting of all these agencies and respective authorities, and 
will take the remedial measures. I will also look into the two specific examples 
that he has brought to my notice and act upon them. 
SHRI B. P. SINGHAL: Sir, the point was that when there is a possibility of 
a project being completed at the rate of Rs. 1 crore worth of job in a month, how 
are we tolerating a lesser performance from any agency, notwithstanding which 
agency is performing? The question is, why are we tolerating inefficient agencies 
in carrying out these works? Why can't we blacklist and get rid of all those 
inefficient agencies so that the things can be done faster and more efficiently? 
That was the first point. Sir, I am glad that I got the answer of my second point. 
However, I would also like to know whether the Minister is intending to reward 
those agencies which have saved money. There are four cases, i.e., Zakhira 
Flyover, G.T. Road Shahdara flyover, Peeragari flyover and ROB-22 at Okhla, 
where the agencies have saved money in construction. Have we given any 
reward to them? If we can't reward the efficient and the better ones, and punish 
the inefficient ones, I do not think the efficient agencies would get 
encouragement for doing better work. 
SHRI ANANTH KUMAR: Sir, half the agencies are under the Union 
Government and half under the State Government of Delhi, but, whatever may 
be the case, I entirely ag ree with the hon. Member's viewpoint. The Urban 
Development Ministry will take note of his anguish and take recourse to penalties 
and blacklisting of those agencies which are doing tardy work. We will be 
6 

[29 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
rewarding those who have done the work at a faster pace. We will do that after 
examination of the case one by one. 
SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Sir, if we look at the information provided 
by the hon. Minister, we will find that the time taken in completing the various 
flyovers in Delhi is eleven months, at the minimum, and 90 months, at the 
maximum. Sir, the way the traffic is increasing in Delhi, it would be difficult in

lakhs. 
Mr. Chairman, looking to the problems of Delhi, why can't the Government 
take a firm decision by itself instead of involving the Delhi Tourism and 
Transport Development Corporation. What business do they have to do with 
the flyovers? Their job is development of tourism in Delhi. The Government 
has been giving them liquor vending licences also, and they are selling liquor 
at unauthorised places. 
Sir, I am surprised, as the hon. Minister has said, that even Delhi Tourism 
is involved in the construction of flyovers. What is the Goverment thinking 
about it? I am saying this because during peak hours, it is not possible to go 
from one point to another. 
SHRI ANANTH KUMAR: Sir, regarding the Delhi Tourism Development 
Corporation, I would say that the question of the hon. Member is right, but the 
address is wrong, 1 would pass on his concern to the Delhi Government, because 
Delhi Tourism Development Corporation comes under the Delhi Government. 
Having said that, I entirely agree with him, I would say that there are three types 
of problems. One is the delay in shifting of the various services, especially 
elecrical services, as well as water and sewage services. Secondly, there is 
multiplicity of authority. Thirdly, there is lack of coordination and planning 
because of the multiplicity of authority. Therefore, I propose to call a meeting 
of all these agencies. Actually, we had conducted a seminar on how to speed up

the construction of flyovers. But, now I would call a meeting and pursue the 
matter. We have the example of Maharashtra and Mumbai, where they got rid of

SHRI SURESH KALMADI: It was done in a haphazard manner. There

SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: Sir, the hon, Minister in his reply, has said

Secondly, we will also be looking at developing the prime land beneath

CAG report on failure of JDSMT scheme 
*484. DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided to do away with the Centrally 
sponsored Integrated Development of Small and Medium Towns (IDSMT) 
scheme; 
(b) whether this scheme was launched in the year 1979-80; 
(c) whether the CAG Report in March, 2001, had criticised Government 
for the scheme's failure to achieve its objectives; 
(d) whether Government have repl aced this with the State Pooled 
Financing Mechanism; and 
(e) the reasons for failure of IDSMT scheme? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION (SHRI ANANTH KUMAR): (a) to (e)A Statement is laid on the 
Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) No, Sir. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) to (e)The Comptroller & Auditor General (CAG) in its Report No. 2 of 
2002 for the year ended 31 st March, 2002 has observed inadequate coverage of 
towns under the Integrated Development of Small and Medium Towns (IDSMT) 
Scheme, non-satisfactory project execution, non-availability of financial 
resources, etc. 
The Pooled Finance Development Fund (PFDF) has been conceived as a 
State Pooled Financing Mechanism and is not a replacement of the IDSMT 
Scheme. It seeks to enable a group of small and medium urban local bodies to 
access domestic capital markets in a cost  effective and efficient manner for 
undertaking urban infrastructure projects through a State/Regional level 
financial intermediary. 
It may not be appropriate to say that the IDSMT Scheme has failed. 
Though there may be delay in project execution and inadequate mobilisation 
of institutional finance in some cases, the Scheme has helped in improving 
infrastructural facilities and creation of durable public assets in the selected 
9 

RAJYA SABHA [29 April, 2002] 
small and medium towns. By promoti ng resources generating schemes it has 
helped, to some extent, in improving the overall financial position of the urban 
local bodies. 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: Mr. Ch airman, Sir, the philosophy of 
development of small and medium towns in the country which started in 
1979-80, under the integrated Development of Small and Medium Towns 
Scheme, is very important. The importance was felt because the population 
growth in large cities was so much, almost 250 per cent, whereas in small towns 
that was 33 per cent. But the reply of the Minister on this important issue is one 
of touch-me-not. On the one side, he says that they are doing a very good job 
and on the other, he says that nothing much is being done. Therefore, I would 
like to know this from the hon. Minister. When 4656 schemes were planned in 
two decades, you could hardly achieve 1200 projects. What is the reasons? 
The second part of my question is, in these ten years also, you planned for 
3686 schemes, projects, in 541 towns whereas you could achieve only 821 
projects. I would like to have a categorical answer. How are you going to do it? 
Do you have any financial problem? Keeping in view the importance of the 
scheme, are you going to get more funds for this scheme or not? 
SHRI AN AN TH KUMAR: Sir, there are different types of problems. No. 1 
is paucity of funds. For example, in the Ninth Plan, there was only Rs. 275 
crores allocated; of course, only Rs. 240 crores was spent. We have proposed 
the allocation in the Tenth Plan to the extent of Rs. 1500 crores. Out of this 
Rs. 1500 crores, it was planned to get Rs. 300 crores every year. This year, out 
of the Rs. 300 crores, we have got only Rs. 105 crores. I will be pursuing it with 
the hon. Finance Minister to give us more allocation for this challenging task. 
That is one part of it. The second part of it is, under the IDSMT, 60 per cent of 
the money is given by the Union Government and 40 per cent of the money is 
given by the State Government. And, nowhere are the State Government coming 
forth with their share of the money and the utilisation certificate. The details of 
the CAG report are in front of us. 
SHRI T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: My second question is this, Sir. The 
Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, in its Report No. 2 of 2002 for the 
year ended 31st March, 2002, has observed inadequate coverage of towns 
under the integrated Development of Small and Medium Towns Scheme, Non-
satisfactory project execution, non-availability of financial resources, etc. On 
10 

[29 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
the one hand, the Minister says so. But, on the other hand, he does not accept 
that this scheme has not been given much importance by this Government. I 
call upon the Minister to assure this thing to this august House. He should not 
lay the blame on the Finance Ministry. It is the responsibility of this Government 
to see that the medium and small towns are given more importance so that the 
people may not migrate to the big towns. 
SHRI AN ANTH KUMAR: Sir, it is very eminent that this Government has 
given more impetus and focus to this programme; and instead of Rs. 275 crores 
allocated during the Ninth Plan, we have proposed Rs. 1500 crores for the Tenth 
Plan. But, the problem is that the implementing authority, in this respect, is the 
State Government. They ha ve to choose and prioritie s the various small and 
medium-level townships, and it has to be implemented there, and for implementing 
the said programme at the State level, they need to give their 40 per cent of the 
share. When they do not give their 40 per cent of the share, how can the 
Government of India release 60 per cent of the share? That is the problem. 
DR. T. SUBB ARAMI REDDY: We are not satisfied with the answer of the 
hon. Minister. By saying so, he is trying to shift the responsibility. 
SHRI ANANTH KUMAR: Sir, we are not shifting any responsibility. I 
assure the House that we are revising the various guidelines. In the revised 
guidelines, instead of five categories of towns, we will be making only three 
categories of towns. Secondly, we will be giving 40 per cent of the total allocation 
for water supply and sanitation only. Thirdly, we will be increasing the project 
cost limits also. Right now, the project cost limits are from Rs. 100 lakhs to 
Rs. 750 lakhs. We are going to review that also. We are proactively pursuing the 
project. But, we require more cooperation from the State Governments.

Statement 
(a) and (b) In such situations involving communal flare up there are

resort to the use of force onApril 07,2002 to disperse a mob about 200 persons

OFFICE MEMORANDUM 
Subject:   Guidelines for qualification of Bidders seeking to acquire stakes in 
Public Sector Enterprises through the process of disinvestment 
Government has examined the issu e of framing comprehensive and 
transparent guidelines defining the crite ria for bidders interested in PSE 
disinvestment so that the parties selected through competitive bidding could 
inspire public confidence. Earlier, criteria like net worth, experience etc. used 
to be prescribed. Based on experience and inconsultation with concerned 
departments, Government has decided to prescrible the following additional 
criteria for the qualification / disqualification of the parties seeking to acquire 
stakes in Public Sector Enterprises through disinvestment:—  
(a) In regard to matters other then the security and integrity of the country, 
any conviction by a Court of Law or indictment / adverse order by a regulatory 
authority that casts a doubt on the ability of the bidder to manage the public 
sector unit when it is disinvested, or which relates to grave offence would 
constitute disqualification. Grave offence is defined to be of such a nature that 
it outrages the moral sense the community. The decision in regard to the nature 
of the offence would be taken on case to case basis after considering the facts of 
the case and relevant legal principles, by the Government. 
(b) In regard to matters relating to the security and integrity of the country, 
any charge-sheet by an agency of the Government / conviction by a Court of 
Law for an offence committed by the bidding party or by any sister concern of 
the bidding party would result in disqualification. The decision in regard to the 
relationship between the sister concerns would be taken, based on the relevant 
facts and after examining whether the two concerns are substantially controlled 
by the same person / persons. 
46 

[29 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) In both (a) and (b) disqualification shall continue for a period that 
Government deems appropriate. 
(d) Any entity, which is disqualified from participating in the 
disinvestment process, would not be allowed to remain associated with it or get 
associated merely because it has preferred an appeal against the order based on 
which it has been disqualified. The mere pendency of appeal will have no 
effect on the disqualification. 
(e) The disqualification criteria would come into effect immediately and 
would apply to all bidders for various disinvestment transactions, which have 
not been completed as yet. 
(f) Before disqualifying a concern, a Show Cause Notice why it should not 
be disqualified would be issued to it and it would be given an opportunity to 
explain its position. 
(g) Henceforth, these criteria will be  prescribed in the advertisements 
seeking Expression of Interest (EOl) from the interested parties. The interested 
parties would be required to provide the information on the above criteria, along 
with their Expressions of Interest (EOl). The bidders shall be required to provide 
with their EOl an undertaking to the effect that no investigation by a regulatory 
authority is pending against them. In case any investigation is pending against 
the concern or its sister concern or ag ainst its CEO or any of its Directors / 
Managers / employees, full details of such investigation including the name of 
the investigating agency, the charge / offence for which the investigation has 
been launched, name and designation of persons against whom the investigation 
has been launched and other relevant in formation should be disclosed, to the 
satisfaction of the Government. For other criteria also, a similar undertaking shall 
be obtained alongwith EOl.

Applications for permission for clinical trials, Bio-equivalence studies 
and marketing of new drugs are examined by the New Drug Division in the 
office of DCG (I). The requirement for granting such approval are specified in 
Rules 122A, 122B, 122C, 122D and 122E and Schedule Y of Drugs and 
Cosmetics Rules. The evaluation of new drug/clinical trial is a complex process 
and varies according to the nature of molecule drug, published data and 
information furnished by applicants. Therefore, depending upon the nature of 
the application, it may take on an averag e more than 5 years for approval of 
investigation New Drug (i.e. a drug molecule not tested on human being 
anywhere in the world) about 1—3 years for the first time approval of the drug 
already approved elsewhere but requiring confirmatory clinical trial and about 
2-3 months for subsequent applications for already approved drugs. This is, 
however, subject to submission of all required data as per provisions of Schedule 
Y of Drug and Cosmetics Rule s. Certain critical drugs e.g. anti-cancer, anti-
HIV etc. which are important from the point of view of public health are also 
cleared on a fast track basis. Permissions are granted after taking into account 
the technical requirements and not on discretion. 
(d) The question of investigation by CB1 does not arise.

Eradication of leprosy 
3495. SHRIMATI VANGAGEETHA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government propose to eradicate leprosy 
through National Leprosy Eradication Programme; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
56 

[29 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) the number of leprosy cases in the country; and 
(d) by when the country could achieve elimination of the disease? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b)The Government of India is 
implementing the National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP) in all the 
States/UTs for the elimination of Leprosy. 
National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP) is a 100% Centrally 
sponsored scheme with the objective of achieving the elimination of leprosy i.e. 
prevalence Rate of less than 1 case per 10,000 population, at national level, by 
March, 2004. 
The details of the Programme are:— 
(i) Decentralization and Institutional Development under which State 
Leprosy Societies have been formed in 27 major States and District 
Leprosy Societies in all the original 557 districts in the country. 
(ii)  Integration of Leprosy services with General Health Care. 
(iii) Two rounds of Modified Leprosy Elimination Campaigns (MLEC) 
for case detection throughout the country during 2001-02 and 
2002-03. 
(iv) Early Leprosy Case Detection and Free Multi Drug Therapy to all 
patients. 
(v) Special Action Projects for elimination of Leprosy (SAPEL) and 
Leprosy Elimination Campaign (LEC) for difficult/inaccessible/ 
under served Rural and Urban areas, respectively. 
(vi) Intensified Public Awareness Campaigns. 
(vii) Training of Health Staffiri disability prevention and care. 
(viii) Training of General Health Care Staff in Leprosy. 
(c) The number of leprosy patients in the country as per reports received 
till 31 st March, 2002, is 4.92 lakhs. 
(d) Government of India is aiming to achieve the elimination of leprosy by 
March, 2004.

Mother and Child Programme 
3501. SHRI C.P. THIRUN AVUKKARASU: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have started Mother and Child Programme aimed 
at reducing the risk of HIV transmission to the new-bom; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the clinical tests of the drug used in the programme have been 
done; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; 
(e) whether side-effects of this drug have been reported by FDA; and 
(0 if so, reaction of Government thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (0 In view of the emerging threat of 
transmission of HIV infection from HIV infected pregnant mother to her baby, 
Government of India has started the Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission 
66 

[29 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Programme, in the country. The feasibility study on prevention of mother to child 
transmission was initiated in March, 2000 in 11 Institutions located in five HIV 
high prevalence States namely: Maharashtra (5),Tamil Nadu (3), Andhra Pradesh 
(1), Karnataka (1), Manipur (1). The first phase of the study has been completed 
in September, 2001. In this phase of the study, short course regimen of 
Azidothymadine (AZT) was administered to pregnant mothers who attended 
ante natal clinics from 36 weeks of gestation and during labour at the above 
institutions. In the second phase of the feasibility study at these centres, single 
dose Nevirapine to both HIV infected mother and baby pair is being administered 
for prevention of mother to child transmission. This drug has an additional 
advantage over Azidothymadine as it is administered in single dose besides 
being cost effective as compared to short course regimen of Azidothymadine. 
Encouraged with the results of the feasibility studies, Government has 
decided to scale up Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission Programme in 
the entire country in a phased manner. In the first phase of the Programme, 
Medical Colleges of the six high prevalence States namely Maharashtra, Tamil 
Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Manipur and Nagaland will be covered 
followed by District Hospitals in these States. In the second phase of the 
programme, Medical Colleges of other States will be covered. 
There have been extensive clinical trials of both the anteritroviral drugs 
i.e. Azidothymadine and Nevirapine world-wide. Both the drugs have been 
found safe for the use in prevention of mother to child transmission of HIV 
infection. Azidothymadine and Nevirapine were included in the WHO model 
list of essential drugs in 1999 solely for indicating the prevention of mother to 
child transmission of HIV infection. 
The World Health Organization (WHO) technical declaration in October, 
2000 carefully revised the available information and concluded that benefits 
of decreasing mother to child transmi ssion with these anteritroviral drugs, 
Prophylaxis, regimens greatly outwayed concern related to development of 
drug resistance. 
The Food and DrugAdministration (FDA), USA reviewed medwatch reports 
of serious adverse events in persons taking Nevirapine for post exposure prophylaxis 
received by Food and Drug Administraiton (FDA). This report summarizes results 
of that analysis and indicates that healthy persons taking abbreviated four weeks 
Nevirapine regimen for post exposure prophylaxis are at risk for serious adverse 
event. It has advised that clinicians should use recommended PEP guidelines and 
dosing instruction to reduce risk of serious adverse events. 
67 

RAJYA SABHA [29 April, 2002] 
However, short term safety ana tolerance of single dose Nevirapine being 
used for mother-to child transmission has been demonstrated in various clinical 
trials conducted World-wise.

products are not encouraged.

3520. DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that some medical experts have expressed the fear 
that by the year 2025, India would rank first in diabetic global burden with about 
60 million diabetic cases; 
82 

[29 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the main causes for massive increase; and 
(c) the preventive steps Government propose to take for arresting the 
increase? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c)According to Indian Council of 
Medical Research, the estimated number of  diabetic patients in the country is 
about 25 million. There is epidemio logical evidence showing increase in 
prevalence of diabetes, particularly in urban areas of the country. As per World 
Health Organisation projections, India will have 57 million diabetic by the 
year 2025 when India will become the country to have the largest number of 
diabetic patients. The various combined factors like population ageing, 
unhealthy diets and obesity and sedentar y life style are mainly reported to be 
responsible for increase in diabetes mellitus. 
Diabetes treatment is done at all levels in the rural health care delivery 
system and urban health care institutions. A pilot project on "Strengthening of 
Bio-Chemical Laboratories and Quality Assurance" was initiated in 1999-2000 
in the States of Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and 
Punjab. The National Diabetes Control Programme has now been merged with 
the Indian Council of Medical Research which has constituted as Expert Group 
to formulate a revised comprehensive plan of action to control diabetes. Central 
Health Education Bureau (CHEB) has also strategies/programme including 
use of powerful electronic media to spread health messages to increase Public 
Health Awareness about diabetes.

Achievement of National Population Policy 
†3528. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the extent to which Government have achieved success to check the 
increasing population in the country; 
(b) whether Government have fixed any target under National Population 
Policy to check the increase in population; and 
(c) if so, the effective steps Government  are taking to achieve the said 
target? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) The decadal growth rate of population 
in the country continued to rise from 13.31 per cent in 1951 to 21.64 per cent 
in 1961 and then it reached all time high of 24.80 per cent in 1971. However, it 
started declining afterwards from 24.66 per cent in 1981 to 23.86 per cent in 
1991 and then 21.34 per cent in 2001. Similar trend were noticed in the average 
annual exponential growth rate of population. From 1.25 per cent in 1951 it 
rose to 1.96 per cent in 1961 then to 2.20 per cent in 1971 and it was at top with 
2.22 per cent in 1981. But it came down to 2.14 per cent in 1991 and further 
dipped to 1.93 in 2001. 
(b) and (c) National Population Policy, 2000 does not mention about 
fixing of targets but lists certain socio-demographic goals to be achieved by 
2010. These are: 
(1) Address the unmet needs for basi c reproductive and child health 
services, supplies and infrastructure. 
(2) Make school education upto age 14 free and compulsory and reduce 
dropouts at primary and secondary school levels to below 20 per 
cent for both and girls. 
†Original notice of (he question was received in Hindi. 
92 

[29 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(3) Reduce infant mortality rate to below 30 per 1000 live births. 
(4) Reduce maternal mortality ratio to below 100 per 100.000 live 
births. 
(5) Achieve universal immunization of children against all vaccine 
preventable diseases. 
(6) Promote delayed marriage for girls, not earlier than age 18 and 
preferably after 20 years of age. 
(7) Achieve 80 percent institutional deliveries and 100 percent 
deliveries by trained persons. 
8) Achieve universal access to info rmation/counseling and services 
for fertility regulation and contr aception with a wide basket of 
choices. 
(9) Achieve 100 per cent registration of births, deaths, marriages and 
pregnancy. 
(10) Contain the spread of Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome 
(AIDS) and promote greater integration between the management 
of Reproductive Tract Infection (RTI) and Sexually Transmitted 
Infections (STI) and the National AIDS Control Organisation. 
(11) Prevent and control communicable diseases. 
(12) Integrate Indian System of Medicines (ISM) in the provision of 
reproductive and chlid health serv ices and in reaching out of 
households. 
(13) Promote vigorously the small family norm to achieve replacement 
levels to TFR. 
(14) Bring about converagcncc in implementation of related social 
sector programmes so that family welfare becomes a people centered 
programme. 
 The effective steps tnken after the adoption of NPP 2000 
are as under: > State Government have been advised to 
formulate State Population Policy with State specific 
strategies while maintaining the general spirit of National

Population Commission under th e chairmanship of Chief 
Minister of respective State to review, monitor and give 
directions for the implementation of the State Population 
Policy with a view to meeting the goals set out in the 
National Population Policy, 2000.

firm and detailed action pl an taking into account the 
ground realities and 

RAJYA SABHA [29 April, 2002]

Use of emergency contraceptive 
3533. SHRI YADLAPATIVENKATRAO: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are shortly introducing an emergency 
contraceptive in urban areas after proper training of doctors" and health workers; 
(b) whether the emergency contraceptive is a new device of family 
planning; 
(ej if so, the salient features thereof; 
(d) whether this contraceptive will be introduced in rural areas also; and 
(e) if so, the details in this regard? 
98 

[29 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (e) The Government of India has 
decided to introduce Emergency Contraceptive Pills under the National Family 
Welfare Programme. The Drug Controller General of India has approved 
levonorgestrel tablets (0.75 mg.) as an emergency contraceptive. The first tablet 
is required to be taken within 72 hours of unprotected sexual act, followed by 
a second tablet to be taken twelve hours later. 
Emergency Contraception is not a concept for planning a family. It refers 
to a modality that is used as an em ergency procedure th at will succeed in 
preventing unwanted pregnancy after any unprotected, possibly fertile sexual 
act. In this case, this modality is an oral contraceptive pill confirming to the 
above specifications. Emergency contraception does not prevent pregnancy 
once implantation has taken place and it cannot be used as a regular contraceptive. 
If used in the event of an unplanned / unwanted pregnancy, it will bring 
about reductions in the incidence of unsafe abortions implemented by 
unqualified personnel under conditions which are not hygienic.

3551. DR. KARAN SINGH: Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND 
BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have identified piracy as the main cause for 
doom for India's film industry; 
(b) whether in this context Government's attention was drawn to the Anti-
piracy Conference organized by the Indian Motion Pictures Producers 
Association and the Motion Pictures Association International in New Delhi 
on March 12, 2002; and

THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING 
(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) The Government shares the concern of 
the Film Industry about the leakage of earnings due to piracy.

Producers' Association (IMPPA) a Conference was jointly organized by them 
with Motion Picture Association-International(MPA) on 12th March, 2002, to 
address the issue of piracy in the entertainment industry and various ways to 
fight the same. 
(c) Enforcement of the Copyright Act lies with the State Governments 
through the police. Ministry of Human Resource Development, the nodal 
Ministry for copyright matters, has directed States/Union Territories to set up 
separate copyright enforcement cells or special cells in the Crime Branch to 
113 

RAJYA SABHA [29 April, 2002] 
exclusively look into co pyright infringement cases . Copyright enforcement 
cells have been set up in most of the States/Union Territory administrations 
headed by a senior police officer to deal with such matters.

this Ministry as a result of the deliberations of the 24th State Information Ministers 
Conference (SIMCONj, has also recommended formulation of appropriate training 
modules for police officers to train them for anti-piracy work. To create an anti-
piracy mind-set, this Ministry has recen tly brought together representatives of 
the film producers, multi-service operators and cable operators who have jointly 
resolved not to exhibit films without valid permission from the copyright holders.

Scope of Lok Adalats 
3573. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of LAW, 
JUSTICE AND COMPANYAFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided to extend the scope of Lok Adalats 
to provide compulsory pre-litigation mechanism for conciliation and settlement 
of cases relating to the public utility services; 
(b) whether Government are proposing to extend the limit of Lok 
Adalats upto Rs. 50 lakhs; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
ARUN JAITLEY): (a) to (c) At present, the Lok Adalats can settle disputes only 
on the basis of compromise or settlement among the parties. If the parties do not 
arrive at a settlement, the case is cither returned to the court of law or the parties 
arc advised to seek remedy in a court of law. To remove this drawback, it has 
been decided to add a new chapter in the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, 
140 

[29 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
which will facilitate setting up of permanent Lok Adalats for providing 
compulsory pre-litigative mechanism for conciliation and settlement of cases 
relating to public utility services. A bill to this effect has already been 
introduced in Lok Sabha. The National Legal Services Authority or the State 
Legal Services Authority, as the case may be, may establish permanent Lok 
Adalat at such places and in such numbe rs as may be expedient to enable the 
Lok Adalats to exercise its jurisdiction in respect of one or more public utility 
services as necessary from time to time. The permanent Lok Adalats would 
have jurisdiction regarding public utility services such as transport (air, road, 
water), postal, telegraph or telephone, power, water, sanitation, hospitals and 
insurance. To avoid prolonged litigation it has also been proposed that the 
award made by the Lok Adalat shall be final, binding and shall not be 
questioned in any original suit, app lication or execution proceeding. The 
jurisdiction of the Lok Adalats would be limited to cases upto a monetary 
value of Rs. 10 lakhs. Under clause 22C of the Legal Services Authorities 
(Amendment) Bill, 2002 which is yet to be passed by Parliament, 
Government has power to increase the limit of ten lakh rupees in consultation 
with National Legal Services Authority.

Statement 
A set of new fundamental Rights for inclusion in Part III of Constitution as 
suggested by National Commission to review the working of the 
Constitution. 
1. In article 12 of the Constitution, the expression "other authorities" 
shall include any person in relation to such of its functions which 
are of a public nature. 
2. In articles 15 and 16, prohibition against discrimination should be 
extended to "ethnic or social origin, political or other opinion, 
properly or birth". 
3. Article I9(l)(a) and (2) should be amended to read as follows:  
Article 19(1): All citizens shall have the right: 
(a) to freedom of speech and expression which shall include the 
freedom of the press and other media, the freedom to hold 
opinions and to seek, receive and impart information and ideas. 
19(2): proposes to give the State powers to impose reasonable restrictions 
of the above right by making suitable laws in the interest of 
sovereignty, integrity, security of the country, etc. 
144 

[29 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
4. The existing article 21 may be re -numbered as clause (1) thereof, 
and a new clause (2) should be inserted thereafter on the following 
lines:—  
"No one shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or 
degrading treatment or punishment." 
5. After clause (2) in article 21, a new clause, namely, clause (3) should 
be added on the following lines:—  
"Every person who has been illegally deprived of his right to life or 
liberty shall have an enforceable right to compensation." 
6. After article 21, a new article, say article 21 -A, should be inserted 
on the following lines:—  
"Every person shall have the right to leave the territory of India 
and every citizen shall have the right to return to India." 
7. A new article, namely, article 21-B, should be inserted on the 
following lines:—  
"Every person has a right to respect for his private and family life, 
his home and his correspondence." 
8. A new article, say article 21 -C, may be added to make it obligatory 
on the State to bring suitable legislation for ensuring the right to 
rural wage employment for a minimum of eighty days in a year. 
9. After article 30, a new article, 30-A, regarding access to Courts 
and Tribunals and speedy justice should be added. 
 
10. Article 39-A, in Part IV under the Directive Principles of State 
Policy, regarding equal justice and free legal aid, should be made 
a Fundamental Right and added as a new article, 30-B of the

(c) by when Government are likely to formulate their views with regard to

before taking a final decision in the matter? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
ARUN JAITLEY): (a) and (b) The National Commission to Reveiw the 
Working of the Constitution has made a number of recommendations on 
"Reforms in electoral process". Details of the recommendations are given in 
the Statement attached (see below). 
(c) Action on the recommendations lies with the Ministries / Departments 
of the Government of India, which are administratively concerned with the subject 
matter of the recommendations. 
(d) the report of the Commission has been made public by putting the 
same on internet so that debate in the public can take place. 
Statement 
Recommendations made by the National Commission to review the 
working of the Constitution on electoral process 
1. Introduction of Electronic Voting Machines in all constituencies. 
2. Empowerment of Election Commission of India to countermand and 
order fresh elections, ordering re-poll in entire constituency. Use of 
tamper-proof video and other electronic surveillance at sensitive stations. 
3. Elections campaigning on caste or religious basis and attempts to 
spread caste and communal hatred be made punishable with mandatory 
imprisonment or even disqualification of the candidates. 
4. Amendment in Representation of People's Act to include tougher 
provision for disqualification of candidates, charged with offences 
punishable with imprisonment of 5 years or more or convicted with 
imprisonment of 6 months or more and derecognition of political 
parties which field such candidates despite being aware of his 
antecedents. 
5. Barring of any person convicted of heinous crimes like murder, rape, 
smuggling, dacoity, etc., perman ently from contesting for any 
political office. 
147 

RAJYA SABHA [29 April, 2002] 
6. Setting Special Courts to dispose criminal cases against politicians 
speedily. Empowering these courts to decide whether there is indeed 
a prima-facie case justifying the framing of charges by the police 
against a potential candidate in a time-bound manner. The special 
courts should be constituted at the level of High Courts and their 
decisions should be appealable before the Supreme Court only. Cases 
should be decided within a period of 6 months. 
7. The provision in sub-section (4) of Section 8 of the Representation of 
People's Act, 1951, should be suitably amended so that the benefit of 
this provision is not available for the purpose of the person contesting 
fresh elections.- 
8. The provision regarding disqualification of a person from contesting 
elections after charges are framed in a Court for an offence 
punishable with imprisonment for a maximum period of 5 years or 
more after expiry of a period of one year should be equally 
applicable to sitting MPs and MLAs. 
9. Restoring the position prevailing before 1975 amendment of the 
Representation of People's Act, 195 1, to enable the President to 
determine the period of disqualification under Section 8A on direct 
opinion of the EC to avoid any delay in the matter. 
10. Special Courts or special election benches in High Courts should 
dispose of election petitions and election disputes. 
11. Matter regarding election expenses and their auditing etc., should be 
rationalized. 
12. All candidates and every holder of a political position must declare 
his assets and liabilities and those of his close relatives at the time of 
elections or annually as the case may be. 
13. Proposals of State funding the election should be deferred till 
regulatory mechanisms are firmly in place. 
14. Campaign period should be reduced considerably. Candidates should 
not be allowed to contest from more than one constituency. Election 
code of conduct should come into operation immediately on 
declaration of elections and violations should be made a penal offence. 
15. The Commission has recommended a careful and full examination of 
the issue of prescribing a minimum of 50% plus one vote for 
148 

[29 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
elections in all its aspects in consultation with various political 
parties and other interested parties. 
16. Inter-State delimitation exercise  of Lok Sabha and Assembly 
constituencies may be undertaken. SC and non-scheduled areas ST 
seats should be rotated. 
17. The Tenth Schedule of the Constitution should be amended to provide 
that all persons who defect, whether individually or in groups, must 
resign from their seats and contest fresh elections. Defectors should 
be debarred from holding any public post or any remunerative 
political post during the remaining term or till fresh elections. The 
vote cast by such defectors should be  treated as invalid and decision 
on disqualification should vest with the Election Commission. 
18. There should be a ceiling of 10 per cent on the number of Ministers 
in a State or the Union Government by making suitable law. Practice 
of creating political offices with perks equivalent to Ministers should 
be discouraged and restricted to 2 per cent of the total strength of the 
Lower House. 
19. Independent candidates should be discouraged. Security Deposits in 
respect of these candidates should be doubled. The deposits should be 
double every progressive year in case they fail to win elections and 
they should be debarred from contesting elections for a period of 6 
years if they fail to get 5 per cent of the total votes cast and debarred 
permanently for failing to win 3 elections. 
20. The limit for forfeiting the security deposit should be increased from 
16.67 per cent to 25 per cent to reduce non-serious candidates. 
21. It should be possible without any constitutional amendment to 
provide for the election of the Leader of the House (Lok Sabha/ State 
Assembly) along with the election of the Speaker and in like manner 
under the Rules of Procedure. The person so elected may be 
apppointed the Prime Minister / Chief Minister. 
22. The issue of eligibility of non-Indian bom citizens or those whose 
parents or grandparents were citizens of India to hold high offices 
in the realm such as President, Vice-President, Prime Minister and 
Chief Justice of India should be examined in depth through a political 
process after a national dialogue. 
149 

RAJYA SABHA [29 April, 2002] 
23. The CEC, other Elections Commissioners should be appointed on the 
recommendation of a body consisting of the PM, Leader of Opposition 
in both the Houses and Speaker and Deputy Chairman of Lok Sabha 
and Rajya Sabha respectively. 
24. Only those persons who have cleared all Government dues should be 
cleared to contest elections. That the matter is pending before a Court 
of law should be no excuse in the matter. 
25. Suitable amendments should be made in the Constitution to empower 
the Election Commission to identif y and declare various offices 
under the Government to be within 'Offices of Profit'.

Economic Developmental activities for the welfare of backward classes 
3598. SHRI BACHANILEKHRAJ: Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any proposal to promote the economic 
developmental .activities for the benefit of the Backward Classes; 
(b) if so, the introduction of various programmes/schemes by the 
Backward Classes finance and Development Corporation to achieve the above 
objectives; and 
(c) the steps taken by the Government of Gujarat and other States since 
the Constitution of the Corporation? 
THE MINISTER OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT 
(DR. SATYA NARAYAN JATIYA: (a) and (b) The Government of India has 
been implementing a Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Assistance to Voluntary 
Organisations for the Welfare of Other Backward Classes (OBCs) since 1998-
99 for economic development of OBCs. In addition, the National Backward 
Classes Finance and Development Corporation (NBCFDC) establish by the 
Government in 1992, is also implementing the following scheme to promote 
economic and developmental activities for the benefit of backward classes 
and to assist the poorer sections of these classes in skill development and for 
setting up self-employment ventures: 
164

(i) Term Loan Scheme 
(ii) Margin Money Loan Scheme 
(iii) Micro Credit Financing Scheme 
(iv) New Swamima Scheme 
(v) Educational Loan Scheme 
(vi) Training Schemes. 
(c) Since its inception, the NBCFDC has disbursed an amount of 
Rs.647.04 crores to cover 4.01 lakhs beneficiaries till date, out of which an 
amount of Rs. 48.45 crores has been disbursed to Gujarat Backward Classes 
Development Corporation to cover 8460 beneficiaries.

Use of rubber bearing in construction 
3615. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of 
URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that  rubber bearing is useful and 
resistant to natural hazards such as earthquake and cyclone and in Japan many 
multi-storey buildings have been supported on rubber bearings isolators; 
(b) if so, whether Government have any plan to use rubber bearings in 
construction of multi-storey buildings for protection from earthquakes; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the steps taken by Government to develop indigenous 
technology for rubber bearing for use in construction industry? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA) : (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The Technical Committee of Bureau of Indian Standards 
dealing with earthquake resistant construction has made following provisions 
in the Foreword of revised Indian Standards IS: 1893 Criteria for Earthquake 
Resistant Design and Construction of Structures Part-I General Provisions of 
Building. 
"Base isolation and energy absorbing devises may be used for 
earthquake resistant design. Only standard devices having detailed 
experimental data on the performance should be used. The designer must 
demonstrate by detailed analyses that  these devices provide sufficient 
protection to the buildings and equipment as envisaged in this Code. 
Performance of locally assembled isolation and enersy 
194 

[29 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
absorbing devices should be evaluated experimentally before they are used in 
practice. Design of buildings and equipment using such device should be 
reviewed by the Competent Authority. 
Base isolation systems are found useful for short period structures, say 
less than 0.7 sec. including soil—structure material".  
The above provision would facilitate  the adoption of such technology 
in the country with due consideration of its performance and quality control. 
Government is open to adopt base isolation technique for buildings 
wherever necessary. As a beginning, recently in Gujarat the new Bhuj hospital 
building has been designed and being constructed using Lead Rubber Bearing 
in collaboration with experts from New Zealand. 
The experience of this building will help in extending the above 
technology to other important structures. 
(d) Possibility of transfer of technology with Malaysia Rubber Board for 
manufacture of rubber bearing is under consideration by the scientific 
community in the country. 
Experts are also engaged in developing guidelines and methods to use 
this technology of base-isolation for different types of buildings in earthquake 
prone regions.

Comprehensive plan for development of slums 
3627. SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government are planning to bring National 
Slum Development Policy; 
(b) if so, whether any comprehensive study has been done, so far, to 
identify the number of slums and the people living therein in the country; and 
(c) if so, whether any comprehensive plan is being considered to develop 
all the slums in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Slum Development being a State subject, State Governments survey 
arid take stock of slums in their respective States. Town and Country Planning 
Organisation (TCPO) under the Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty 
Alleviation conducted a one time study on slums in 1995-96 and brought out 
a report titled "A Compendium on Indian Slums—1996" and according to this 
report the identified/estimated urban slum populations in the country for 1991 
and 2001 was 462.608 lakhs and 618.258 lakhs respectively. 
An attempt has also been made for the first time during the Census of 
India, 2001 by the Registrar General of India to collect detailed data about 
slum areas of the country particularly in cities/towns having 50,000 population 
or more, based on 1991 census, and as per the provisional figures of Census of 
India, 2001 the slum population of the country is 406.05 lakhs as reported from 
only 607 towns/cities all over India. 
(c) The problem of slum dwellers has been engaging the attention of 
Government since the 2nd Five Year Plan. A number of programmes/schemes 
were launched by the Government for improving the economic and 
environmental conditions of the slum dwellers living all over the country. 
Some of the important programmes are as under:—  
The Environmental Improvement of Urban Slums (EIUS) scheme is in 
operation in the States Sector through which basic facilities like water supply, 
sewerage, storm water drains, community facilities, widening and paving of 
paths/lanes, street lighting are provided in the existing slums by the State 
Governments. 
209 

RAJYA SABHA [29 April, 2002] 
During 1996 to ameliorate the living condition of slum dwellers the 
Central Government launched a scheme namely National Slum Development 
Programme (NSDP), under which the funds are provided by the Central 
Government in the form of Additional Central Assistance (ACA) for provision 
of basic amenities like water supply, storm water drains, community bath, 
widening and paving existing lanes, sewers, community,latrines, street light 
etc. including provision of community centres, to be used for pre-school 
education, non-formal education, adult education, recreational activities etc. 
in improving the condition of slum dwellers in States/Union Territories. 
A scheme called Swama Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) which 
seeks to provide gainful employment to the unemployed and underemployed 
poor, as per guidelines of the scheme, is under implementation since 1. 12.1997. 
A new scheme called Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana (VAMBAY) has 
been launched in December, 2001 to provide shelter/shelter up-gradation to 
the slum dwellers living below poverty line including economically weaker 
sections. This scheme has a component for providing community toilet facility 
also to slum dwellers. The Central Government provides subsidy to the projects 
of the State Governments to the extent of 50% while the balance amount is to 
be met by the State Governments either through loans from HUDCO or other 
agencies or contribution from any other source.

DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to refer to 
Unstarred Question 2355 given in the Ra jya Sabha on 11th December, 2000 
and state: 
(a) whether inspite of the assurance no efforts have been made to allot 
land to Jhuggi cluster till date; 
(b) whether the squatters of Alknanda Camp are now encroaching the 
pavements and spreading on the main road giving a very ugly look to the posh 
and educational area; 
(c) whether no public utility services viz. CGHS, post office, barat ghar, 
community centre are available to the residents of huge DDA apartments; and 
(d) if so, by when the jhuggi dwellers between Mandakini and Aravali 
Apartments will be shifted to make the place hygienic for residents and 
educational institutions? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) DDA has reported that the relocation of jhuggies from 
Alaknanda Camp is in its priority. The survey of JJ cluster, Alaknanda Camp 
has been started for relocation purpose. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
213 

RAJYA SABHA [29 April, 2002] 
(c) Sites meant for public utilities viz. CGHS, post office, barat ghar, 
community hall etc. are presently encroached by jhuggi dwellers. Provision of 
these services would be possible after relocation of jhuggi dwellers from these 
sites. 
(d) DDA has indicated that the said cluster is expected to be shifted soon. 
However, no specific time frame can be indicated at this stage. 
Irregularities in Mohannagar Karamchari Sehkari Avas Samiti, 
Ghaziabad 
3634. SHRI GANDHI AZAD: Will the  Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have received any representation in respect of 
irregularities and corruption in Mohannagar Karamchari Sehkari Avas Samiti, 
Mohannagar, Ghaziabad; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the action taken/proposed to be taken in the matter? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) and (b) As per the information received from the U.P. 
Housing and Development Board, it had received complaints, the brief of which 
are as under:—  
(i) The development works of the Samithi were got done through 
the U.P. Housing and Development Board. Samithi on its own 
had decided to charge Rs. 800/- per sq.mtr. as development 
charges and Rs. 200/- per sq.mtr. had been demanded as land 
cost, instead of Rs. 40/- per sq.mtr. as land cost. 
(ii) Samithi had not prepared any income and expenditure details 
on annual basis. From 1982 onwards no balance sheet had been 
prepared and no general body meeting was called. The members 
are not informed of the monthly expenditure details for the years 
from 1998-99 to 2000-2001. The details of the development 
expenditure and other miscellaneous expenses incurred through 
the U.P. Housing and Development Board have not been 
intimated to the members. 
214 

[29 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(iii) Without the approval of General Body, an amount of Rs. 350/-
per sq.mtr. as additional development expenditure and Rs. 10/-
per sq.mtr. as maintenance expenditure is being demanded from 
the members of the Samithi. 
(iv) Election to the Prabandh Committee by the General Body was 
not conducted in a democratic manner. 
(c) As per the information received from the U.P. Housing and Development 
Board, the complaints were got investigated by the Cooperative Officer 
(Housing) Ghaziabad. As per the investigation report, the complaints on various 
aspects were found not to be correct.

Melting of Glaciers 
†*470. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of 
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Government are aware that about fifteen thousand small 
and big glaciers in the Himalayan region are melting so fast, due to which the 
country could face severe water crisis in the next ten years; 
(b) if so, what strategy Government have decided to adopt in this regard; 
and 
(c) what steps Government are taking to stop melting of glaciers, so that 
flow of water therefrom in Ganga, Yamuna and Brahmputra rivers continue to 
be available? 
THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (c) Yes, the Government are aware of the fact that the 
Glaciers in the Himalayan region are shrinking gradually. As per the inventory 
of Himalayan Glaciers prepared by Geological Survey of India, there are over 
7500 glaciers (big and small) in the Indian part of the Himalaya. The recession 
of glaciers is a natural process sensitive to climatic fluctuation wherein the rise 
in global average temperature (called global warming) results in melting of the 
glaciers in extents varying with their locations as well as seasons. 
The studies carried out in Himalayan Region have indicated that these 
Glaciers are passing through a phase of recession. The rate of recession in 
different climatic zones of the Himalaya is found to be different in different 
years. Studies indicate that during the coming ten years, the rate of recession is 
not likely to reach an extent which could cause water scarcity. The measures 
taken to reduce the effect of human interference on glaciers include conservation 
activities such as afforestation, removal of garbage and promotion of sustainable 
eco-tourism.

several scientific disciplines like Phys ics, Botany, Chemistry, Mathematics,

Climate changes in agriculture 
3329. SHRI MAN MOHAN SAM AL: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that many parts of Orissa are going drier day by day, 
affecting the agricultural sector adversely; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor and the measures taken by Government in 
respect thereof; 
(c) whether Government have made any specific study to assess the impact 
of climatic changes on the agricultural sector of Orissa; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (d) According to India 
Meteorological Department, who among other subjects also deal with the subject 
of climatology, there is no evidence of a long term decreasing trend in rainfall 
of Orissa. However, the State exhibits a high degree of year-to- year variability 
of rainfall in certain districts. 
Several long term measures are being taken by the State Government to 
improve the efficiency of water use. These are:—  
(1) Minor Irrigation sources with emphasis on conjunctive use of 
surface and ground water are bein g developed in a big way by 
availing funds from various sources like loan from NABARD under 
RIDF and central schemes. About 25 thousand shallow tube wells, 
bore wells and river lifts have been installed during the last few 
years. Pani Panchayats are activat ed through farmer's participation 
for rationalizing the use of irrigation water. 
(2) As paddy is the main crop that is affected by the failure of the rains, 
fanners are being motivated to diversify from high water using crop 
like paddy to low water consuming crops like pulses and oilseeds. 
249

(3) Dry land farming methods are being propagated with emphasis on 
drought resistant Agricultural crops and Horticulture crops. Agro 
forestry crops also are being propagated. Mixed farming systems are 
also encouraged.

      are being taken up under Watershed Mission specially created for  
this purpose.

Subsidy to fertilizer companies 
3355. SHRI SANJAYNIRUPAM: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are paying huge amounts of subsidy to fertilizer 
companies in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government are planning to cut that subsidy; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS (SHRI SATYA BRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) and (b) Government 
provides subsidy on urea, which is the only fertilizer under statutory price, 
distribution and movement control, in terms of the provisions of Retention 
Price-cum-Subsidy Scheme. Besides, Government provides concession on 
decontrolled phosphatic and potassic fertilizers under the Concession Scheme 
for decontrolled phosphatic and potassic fertilizers. Government fixes the 
Maximum Retail Price (MRP) in case of urea and indicates MRPs in case of 
decontrolled P&K fertilizers. The MRPs of Single Super Phosphates are 
indicated by respective St ate Governments. Since MRP/indicative MRPs are 
less than the cost of production of fertilizers, fertilizer  manufacturers are 
compensated by payment of subsidy/concession as the difference between the 
normative cost of production plus 12% post tax return on net worth and the 
MRP/indicative MRPs. While in the case of decontrolled phosphatic and 
potassic fertilizers, manufacturers are given concession at uniform rates, but in 
the case of urea, which is the only controlled fertilizer, payment of subsidy is 
determined unit-wise under the provisions of RPS. During 2001-2002, the 
Government has made payments of Rs. 8297.44 crore on subsidy on urea and 
Rs. 4504.00 crore on concession on decontrolled phosphatic and potassic fertilizers. 
(c) and (d) Government is making the system of subsidy disbursement 
more transparent and rational which will encourage the units to improve 
efficiency and reduce costs. In keeping with the policy of economic liberalisation 
and reforms, all other varieties of fertilizers except urea have already been freed 
from price, movement and distribution control. The Government intends moving 
towards a deregulated regime in all the three types of fertilizers, that is, nitrogen, 
phosphatic and potassic, after taking into account its fiscal capacity on the one 
hand and making available fertilizers to the farmers at a reasonable price on the 
other.

3373. SHRI K.B. KRISHNA MU RTHY: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the frame-work for evalua tion and approval of Genetically

Environment Protection Act, which need s a relook, in view of the recent 
developments in molecular biotechnology; and

and Genetic Engg. Approval Committee; if so, whether Government would 
create a unified regulatory authority? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) The biosafety regulatory framework in India consists of 
the Rules for the Manufacture, Use, Import, Export and Storage of Hazardous 
Microorganisms/Genetically Engineered Organisms or Cells, 1989 made by 
the Ministry of Environment and Forests under the Environment (Protection) 
Act, 1986, and the guidelines issued by the Department of Biotechnology. The 
Government is following a policy of case by case approval of transgenic crops. 
Introduction of any new technology requires careful evaluation and long term 
sustainable benefits. Extensive Rules and guidelines have been made for 
evaluating the environmental and health safety aspects of genetically modified 
organisms. Any company involved in the use of genetic engineering techniques 
has to obtain the approval of the Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation 
282 

[29 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(RCGM) set up under the 1989 Rules in the Department of Biotechnology for 
testing under laboratory conditions and confined field conditions. Thereafter, 
approval of GEAC is required for large scale field trials and introduction in the 
environment. This evaluation process is  not cumbersome an d protracted, and 
is necessary to adequately address the sa fety concerns of release of such GM 
products into the environment.

BAALU): (a) to (0 The Supreme Court in its order dated 5th April, 2002, in

Kyoto Protocol on Environment 
3382. DR. KARAN SINGH: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether bending over backwards, Government have welcomed the 
US Policy on climate change, opposing the Kyoto Protocol, which has all 
along been opposed by India as a pioneer of the cause of the developing world; 
(b) if so, the details of the Kyoto Protocol, the stand taken by the US 
thereupon, and Government's decision in regard thereto; and 
290 

[29 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) how the US stand, taken to its logical conclusion would affect the 
global environment and emission of Green House Gas level on the global 
ecology and atmosphere? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU); (a) to (c) India has not welcomed US opposition to Kyoto Protocol 
and would continue to work with the international community in furtherance 
of the Bonn Agreement and Marrakech Accord for early ratification and entry 
into force of the Kyoto Protocol. There has been no change in India's policy on 
climate change, which is based on maintenance of present equilibrium of 
commitments and differentiation between developed and developing countries 
wilh no new commitments for the developing countries. 
The Kyoto Protocol commits the developed countries to reduce emissions 
of Green House gases by an average of 5.2% below 1990 levels during 2008— 
2012. It also provides for three mechanisms, i.e. Joint Implementation, Clean 
Development Mechanism and Emission Trading that enable the developed 
countries with quantified emission limitation and reduction commitments to 
acquire Green House gas reduction credits from outside their own boundaries 
at relatively lesser costs to facilitate compliance with the Green House limitation 
and reduction commitments. It further provides for a compliance mechanism to 
address cases of noncomplia nce with the provisions of Protocol. The United 
States of America has expressed its opposition to Kyoto Protocol on the grounds 
of economic burden it would impose on its economy, exemption of major 
developing countries like India and China from specific commitments and 
scientific uncertainty. 
United States of America is the largest emitter of Green House gases in the 
world. In 1990, it alone accounted for over 36% of developed country emissions 
and its emissions have continued to grow. The Kyoto Protocol provides for 
emission reduction commitment of 7% for the United States with reference to 
1990. The opposition of United States to Kyoto Protocol would adversely affect 
global efforts to reduce Green House gas emissions and combat climate change.

3409. SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO: W ill the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the percentage of non-utilisation of 1999-2000 
and 2000-2001, BE allocation for strengthening ofTeachers Training Institutes 
and National Council ofTeachers Education were around 32 per cent and 13 per 
cent, as well as 27 per cent and 43 per cent, respectively; 
(b) if so, the percentages of non-utilisation in 2001-2002 in case of these 
two programmes; 
(c) what are the reasons for such non-utilisation; and 
(d) whether Government propose to meet the targets of teachers' training 
with reduction of around 15 per cent and 25 per cent, respectively, in BE 2002-
2003 for these two programmes? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) Yes Sir. 
(b) and (c) The percentage of non-utilisation in 2001-2002 is 22 percent 
under the Scheme of Restructuring an d Reorganisation of Teacher Education 
and 25 per cent in NCTE. The non- utilisation of amount provided in the BE is 
due to (i) the fact that activities such as teacher training and research are also 
being funded under the District Primary Education Programme and Sarva Shiksha 
Abhiyan (ii) availability of unspent balance with the State and UT Governments 
under the scheme of Restructuring an d Reorganisation of Teacher Education 
and also with NCTE (iii) delays in construction works undertaken in the scheme 
and (iv) delay in preparation of appropriate proposals by State Governments.

Hence there will be no fund constraint in meeting targets. With unspent amount 
lying with the State and UT Governments and also with NCTE, the reduction in 
BE 2002-2003 may not affect the activities and the programmes during the year.

Banning the use of children as soldiers 
3411. SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India has not taken any decision so far regarding the United 
Nations Treaty for banning the use of children as soldiers, a major violation of 
human rights; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) the details of the United Nations Treaty; and 
(d) how many countries have agreed to implement the same? 
322 

[29 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE INTHE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SUMITRAMAHAJAN): (a) to (d)The Optional 
Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child involving children in 
armed conflict obliges State Parties to take feasible measures to ensure that 
minimum age of recruitment to armed forces is raised to 15 years and that the 
members of their armed forces, who have not attained the age of 18 years, do 
not take a direct part in hostilities and also to ensure that the persons, who have 
not attained the age of 18 years, are not compulsorily recruited into their armed 
forces. As per the information received from Ministry of Defence the minimum 
age of recruitment of soldiers in the army is 16 years. Persons recruited undergo 
basic military training for upto two and a half years from the date of enrolment 
and are then inducted into regular service. No recruit below the age of 18 years 
is deployed in armed conflict. There is no compulsory recruitment in India. 
According to the UNICEF website only 18 countries have ratified the Protocol. 
The implications of ratification are receiving the attention of Government.

(d) if so, the reasons therefor and whether Government propose to post 
such professors in Shillong who have not been so far posted in NER, in order to 
fill up the vacant posts? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE INTHE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERM A]: (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) A copy of the transfer/posting policy with regard to teachers etc. in the 
Kendriya Hindi Sansthan, Agra, as approved by the then Union Deputy Minister 
of Education & Vice-Chairman of Kendriya Hindi Shikshan Mandal, is enclosed. 
(Seebelow). 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. Dr. Aakurati Gayatri, Reader, after taking over charge 
in the Shillong Centre of the Sansthan, proceeded on long leave on medical 
grounds. Another Senior Lecturer, Dr. Manju Roy was transferred from the 
Shillong Centre of the Sansthan to the Delhi Centre on humantarian grounds. 
Teachers will be posted to the Shillong Centre keeping in view the Sansthan 
transfer guidelines, administrative suitability and academic requirements. 
Statement 
Guidelines for transfer of Teachers of Kendriya Hindi Sansthan, Agra 
(1) Sansthan will ensure that the posts are to be filled up in accordance 
with the sanctioned posts at the H eadquarter and at all the centres. 
The number of teachers in excess to the sanctioned strength shall be 
transferred to the Headquarters/other centres as per requirement. 
327 

RAJYA SABHA [29 April, 2002] 
(2) Transfer from the Agra Headquarter of the Sansthan to Delhi Centre 
or vice-versa shall not be treated equiva lent to other transfers viz. 
transfers from Hyderabad, Myso re, Shi Hong, Guwahati shall be 
treated under a different category which will be applicable to all. 
(3) No transfer shall be made during the academic session as far as 
possible. Efforts will be made to make the transfers effective before 
the commencement of academic session i.e. June. 
(4) The person concerned shall be informed about the transfer two months 
in advance either verbally or in writing so that the person can make 
necessary arrangements therefor. 
(5) All efforts will be made to follow the policy of Government of India 
in respect of posting of husband and wife working in the Sansthan or 
Government of India, at same place. 
(6) The written request for transfer on the basis of mutual consent of the 
teachers shall be considered subj ect to smooth functioning of the 
Institute. The Director will ensure that due to the mutual transfer, the 
better claim of a person, if any, could not be over looked. 
(7) Travelling allowance, tr ansfer grant, joining time etc. shall not be 
allowed to the teachers granted transfer on request. 
(8) Teachers to be appointed at a cer tain centre on the basis of 
advertisement, would be posted at  the same centre. But after three 
years he would be liable to be transferred anywhere as per needs. 
(9) If a teacher is appointed to higher  posts (Lecturer to Reader and 
Reader to Professor), he would be, as per needs, posted at any centre 
of the Institute (i) Shillong, (ii) Guwahati, ( iii) Mysore, (iv) 
Hyderabad, and he would have to serve at that centre. 
(10) Those teachers whose retirement period is less than 3 years, would 
not be transferred as far as possible provided the concerned teacher 
is reluctant. 
(11) The teacher who have not yet been transferred and have been working 
at the same place for more than te n years, would be transferred to 
Shillong or Guwahati Centre for at least two years period. Later, 
328

effort will be made to facilitate him/her to come back to Headquarters 
(Agra)/Hyderabad/Mysore. 
(12) While making appointments to hi gher posts, a Professor will be 
accorded the advantage of his/her service period at Shillong and 
Guwahati centre. 
(13) Officers/Teachers having Institute's accommodation, if transferred 
to Guwahati and Shillong, would have the facility to retain

Peace studies in schools 
3427. DR. KARAN SINGH: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DE VELOPM ENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a proposal to start peace studies in schools has been received 
from UNESCO; 
(b) if so, the details thereof, including the content of the studies and the 
mode of introduction thereof; and 
(c) Government's response thereon? 
THE MIN1STER OF STATE INTHE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) to (c) No formal 
proposal has been received from UNESCO to start "peace studies" in schools. 
However, educationists from India, Pakistan, Bhutan, Maldives and Sri Lanka 
at the Conference on Curriculum Development on Peace Education organised 
in Colombo by UNESCO in January, 2000 had recommended that  peace 
education should be an integral part of the general education of all children in 
340 

[29 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
their own countries and South Asia at large. In pursuance of these 
recommendations a Teacher's Guide to Peace Education has been published with 
UNESCO support. It was launched in India by UNESCO in collaboration with the 
Parliamentarians Forum on 11th March, 2002. 
2. This is an attempt to encourage Member States of UNESCO to formulate 
policies to institutionalize and implement the peace education programmes in 
their respective countries. It clarifies the scope, goals, core values and concepts 
of education and suggests a thematic  model on which a school education 
programme could be designed, implemented and evaluated. This programme is 
basically a character building intervention based on a human, civic, moral and 
spiritual value system with stress on de veloping peaceful living competencies 
in children. Besides identifying characteristics, attitudes and skills necessary 
to be a Peace Teacher, it provides learning activities useful for educating peace 
and points out ways of infusing peace values, attitudes and skills in the formal 
teaching and learning in the classroom along with the ways of eliminating 
violence in school, in all forms. 
3. Elements of peace education have al ways formed part of the Indian 
education system. The National Policy on Education lays considerable emphasis on 
value education by highlighting the need to make education a forceful tool for the 
cultivation of social and moral values. The policy states that in our culturally plural 
society, education should foster universal and eternal values, oriented towards 
unity and integration of our people. 
4. The school curriculum in 1988 was designed to enable the learner to 
acquire knowledge to develop concepts and inculcate values commensurate with 
the social, cultural, economic and environmental realities at the national and 
international levels. The social values aimed at were friendliness, 
cooperation, compassion, self-discipline, courage, love of social justice, etc. 
5. The National Curriculum Framework for School Education 2000 also 
provides that the schools must strive to restore and sustain the universal and eternal 
values towards the unity and integration of people, their moral and spiritual growth 
enabling them to realise the treasure within. It provides for value based education 
which would help the nation fight against all kinds of fanaticism, ill-will, violence, 
fatalism, dishonesty, avarice, corruption, exploitation and drug abuse. 
341 

RAJYA SABHA [29 April, 2002] 
6. This Guide to Peace Education could be used to supplement our efforts 
under the Education in Human Values Programme in our schools. It is proposed 
to prepare a brief version of the Guide suited to the Indian conditions alongwith 
model Teaching & Learning Material (TLM) for use in our DIETs in the Teacher 
Training Programmes.
